title: Get paid to “boost” products online
setup: You mentioned to friends that you want extra income. Out of nowhere, a text arrives.

messages.text: Hi, I'm Lisa, a recruiter with Optima Digital. We saw your resume online. Remote part-time: earn $200–$800/day doing simple app optimization tasks. Interested? Reply YES.
Great! Complete 40 tasks to earn commission. Some premium task sets need a small crypto deposit to unlock, which is refunded with your earnings 💰

options.label: Deposit $100 to unlock the premium tasks
options.feedback: Each “premium set” needed a bigger deposit. The earnings on screen were fake, and none of your money came back.

options.label: Stop replying. Real jobs never make you pay to earn
options.feedback: Unexpected job texts plus depositing your own money to “unlock” pay is the definition of a task scam.

options.label: Do the free tasks only and take the small payout
options.feedback: They'll pay you a few dollars to hook you. Staying in means more pressure to deposit.

redFlags: Unexpected job offer by text or WhatsApp
You have to deposit money, often crypto, to get paid
safestAction: Ignore unexpected job texts. Never pay money to get a job or to unlock earnings.

title: New job sends a check for home-office gear
setup: You applied to remote jobs online. After a text-chat “interview,” you get an offer.

content.subject: Offer of Employment — Remote Data Entry Clerk
content.body:
Congratulations! You've been selected for the position at $32/hour.

We've mailed you a check for $2,950 to purchase your laptop and software from our approved vendor. Deposit it via mobile deposit and send payment to the vendor today so your equipment ships before your start date.
content.footer: Brightpath Solutions · An Equal Opportunity Employer

options.label: Deposit the check and pay the vendor
options.feedback: The check was fake and bounced. The “vendor” was the scammer, and the bank held you responsible.

options.label: Look up the company yourself and call its main number to verify
options.feedback: The real company had no such job. Legit employers don't hire by text chat or send checks to buy equipment.

options.label: Send them your bank login so they can direct-deposit instead
options.feedback: Your login let them drain your account. No employer needs your password.

redFlags: Interview held only by text chat
HR emailing from a free Outlook address
Check to buy equipment from “their” vendor
safestAction: Verify job offers by contacting the company through its official website. Never deposit a check and send money on.

title: Mystery shopper assignment with a check
setup: An envelope arrives with a letter and a check made out to you.

content.subject: Congratulations, you've been selected as a Mystery Shopper!
content.body: Enclosed is a check for $1,980. Deposit it today. Keep $300 as your fee. Use the remaining $1,680 to purchase gift cards at a local store to evaluate the customer service, then text us photos of the card numbers for your report.
content.footer: Complete within 48 hours to remain eligible.

options.label: Deposit the check, buy the gift cards, and send the numbers
options.feedback: The check was fake. The gift card money went to the scammer, and your bank took back the deposit.

options.label: Shred it. Real mystery shopping never involves buying gift cards for them
options.feedback: Check plus gift cards equals scam every time. Well spotted.

options.label: Deposit the check but wait before buying anything
options.feedback: You didn't send money, but depositing a fake check can cause bank fees and account problems.

redFlags: Check comes with instructions to buy gift cards
safestAction: Never deposit a check from a stranger and send money or gift cards back.

title: Interview invite after you applied
setup: Last week you applied for a marketing role on a company's own careers page. This email arrives.

content.subject: Harbor Foods — Marketing Coordinator interview
content.body:
Hi Sam,

Thanks for applying for the Marketing Coordinator role (Req #4471). We'd like to set up a 30-minute video interview with the hiring manager. Please pick a time that works for you through our scheduling page, or reply with your availability.

Best,
Priya

options.label: Confirm the recruiter on the company's site or LinkedIn, then schedule
options.feedback: It matches a job you applied to, comes from the company's domain, and asks for nothing sensitive. Verifying was a smart extra step.

options.label: Ignore it — recruiters who email are always scams
options.feedback: This one was real. You missed an interview for a job you wanted.

options.label: Reply with your SSN and bank info to speed up onboarding
options.feedback: Even real employers collect that only after a formal offer, through secure HR systems — never by email reply.

redFlags: Matches a specific job you applied to
Company email domain and requisition number
Video interview with a real manager; no payment or personal info requested
safestAction: Real recruiters ask for your time, not your money. Verify the person and domain, and share sensitive info only after a formal offer.

title: Get paid $600/week to wrap your car in ads
setup: A post in a local community group catches your eye.

content.body: 🚗 EARN $600/WEEK just for driving! A major energy drink brand will pay you to put their logo on your car. No experience needed. Comment “INTERESTED” and we'll DM you!

options.label: Sign up. When the check comes, pay the “wrap installer” from it
options.feedback: The check was fake. The money you forwarded to the “installer” came out of your own account.

options.label: Skip it and check the brand's official website for any real program
options.feedback: Brands don't recruit random drivers through group posts and send checks to forward. You avoided a fake-check scam.

options.label: Comment “INTERESTED” to learn more
options.feedback: No loss yet, but you just raised your hand for a flood of scam DMs.

redFlags: Easy money for almost no work
Known pattern: a check you must partly send on
safestAction: If you get paid by check and asked to send part of it to someone, it's a scam.
